title: India, UAE Launch Third Mountain Guardian Exercise in Uttarakhand Hills
excerpt: The fortnight-long exercise, running October 5–18 at the Foreign Training Node in Chaubatia, brings 92 troops from both armies together for mountain warfare drills including drone operations and surveillance-grid training.
body:
• The third edition of the India-UAE joint military exercise Mountain Guardian 2026 began on Monday, October 5, at the Foreign Training Node in Chaubatia, Uttarakhand. It runs until October 18, with a focus on mountain warfare and sub-conventional operations.
  • Ninety-two personnel are taking part — 46 from each army. India's contingent is drawn from a Bhairav Battalion; the UAE's from a Mountain Infantry Battalion. Women officers and combatants from both sides are serving in specialist roles.
  • Training covers joint planning, tactical drills, firing practice, surveillance-grid operations, drone employment, rock climbing, obstacle training, endurance exercises and integrated field manoeuvres, with an emphasis on technology-enabled operations.
  • The exercise caps a busy stretch of India-UAE defence engagement: the two countries held their 10th Navy Staff Talks in Abu Dhabi on September 16–17, focused on maritime security and training exchanges.

India and the United Arab Emirates began a fortnight-long joint military exercise on Monday focused on mountain warfare, with troops from both countries training together in the high-altitude terrain of Uttarakhand. Exercise Mountain Guardian 2026, the third edition of the series, is being held at the Foreign Training Node in Chaubatia from October 5 to 18, the Indian Army's Additional Directorate General of Public Information said.

"The exercise will further strengthen interoperability between the two Armies in sub-conventional operations and reinforce the growing India-UAE defence partnership."

— Indian Army, Additional Directorate General of Public Information

What the exercise involves

A total of 92 personnel are participating, with equal representation from both armies. The Indian contingent comprises troops from a Bhairav Battalion, while the UAE contingent is drawn from a Mountain Infantry Battalion. Women officers and combatants from both armies are taking part in a range of specialist roles — a point all official reporting on the exercise has highlighted as reflecting the growing operational role of women in both forces.

The training programme is deliberately demanding. The two sides will conduct joint operational planning, tactical drills, firing practices, establishment of surveillance grids and drone operations, alongside physical endurance training, rock climbing, obstacle training and integrated field manoeuvres. The emphasis, per the Army's statement, is on technology-enabled operations and the exchange of tactics, techniques and procedures for fighting in difficult mountainous terrain — exactly the environment Chaubatia's high-altitude training node is designed to replicate.

Why mountain warfare, and why now

Mountain operations are among the hardest forms of warfare: altitude, weather, restricted mobility and thin supply lines all punish armies that haven't trained together. For India, with the world's most experienced high-altitude force on its northern borders, sharing that expertise is a form of strategic currency. For the UAE, which has been expanding its defence partnerships across Asia, the exercise is a structured way to build mountain-operation competence it does not need at home but may need in coalition operations abroad.

The exercise is also part of a broader, quickening tempo of India-UAE defence engagement. Last month, the two navies held their 10th Navy Staff Talks in Abu Dhabi on September 16–17, co-chaired by Cmde Kartik Srimal and the UAE Navy's Staff Brig Obaid Mubarak Al Ghfeli. Those talks covered operational engagements, training exchanges, maritime security and professional interactions, with both sides committing to deepen the bilateral naval partnership. Mountain Guardian extends that logic from sea to mountain.

The defence partnership in context

The India-UAE relationship has moved steadily beyond its trade-and-energy core over the past decade. Regular army, navy and air force engagements now sit alongside intelligence-sharing and counterterrorism cooperation. Mountain Guardian, launched as a formalised joint exercise series, is one of the more visible symbols of that military-to-military track — and the third edition signals it has settled into the calendar as a recurring event rather than a one-off gesture.

The timing also matters. With security environments across West Asia and South Asia in flux, both countries are investing in interoperability with partners who might operate alongside them in a crisis. Exercises like this one — small, focused, and built around realistic terrain — are where that interoperability is actually earned, in the words of defence analysts who track the series.

What to watch

The exercise runs through October 18, when a closing ceremony will cap the integrated field manoeuvres. Beyond the fortnight itself, watch for the fourth edition's announcement and for whether the exercise grows in scale or adds an air component — a natural next step given both countries' helicopter fleets and the centrality of air support to mountain operations. Either way, the India-UAE defence track has clearly become one of New Delhi's busiest.

nri_angle: The UAE hosts one of the world's largest overseas Indian communities, and a deeper military partnership adds a hard-security pillar to a relationship that already binds the two countries on trade, energy, and people-to-people ties.
